newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia charges ex-naval chief in anti-graft sweep.
newsitem.headline: Russia charges ex-naval chief in anti-graft sweep.

text.p: Russian military prosecutors have charged the former chief of the navy's general staff with abusing his position, the latest senior military official to be caught in a government anti-corruption sweep.

Naval Prosecutor Major-General Valery Suchkov told Itar-Tass news agency on Tuesday that Admiral Igor Khmelnov had been charged with diverting funds meant for naval housing and development of Russia's far eastern naval base.
Khmelnov is alleged to have used money from the sale of 64 warships to India and South Korea to rehouse 273 selected servicemen and their families, Tass said.
Interfax news agency said Khmelnov and his relatives were among the recipients.

At the time, Khmelnov headed the Pacific Fleet, but he moved on to become chief of staff of the Russian navy. The Fleet's prosecutors opened a case against him in February and he was sacked by President Boris Yeltsin in April.

Khmelnov was not immediately available for comment on the newly-laid official charges, which fall under an article in the criminal code on "abuse of official position", carrying a possible jail term of up to 10 years.

Yeltsin last month lashed out at corruption in the armed forces, reflecting the public perception that many generals are more interested in getting the military to build them flashy country villas than in defending Russia.
Many conscripts and even officers, meanwhile, have to put up with primitive accommodation which is sometimes no more than a tent or dugout.
The armed forces have declined dramatically since the collapse of communism shifted Russia's priorities away from a military build-up towards reform of its stricken economy.
But Yeltsin said the problems, which include an acute lack of equipment, delays in the payment of officers' wages and even food shortages, were exacerbated by corruption.
"The soldier is losing weight while the general is getting fatter," Yeltsin told a meeting of military top brass. "They have built dachas for themselves all over the country."

Prosecutor General Yury Skuratov said last month that his office was processing 18 cases against generals alone, including a deputy defence minister and the commanders and deputy commanders of the ground forces and Northern Fleet.
"The list is impressive, which shows that the situation in the army is not normal," Skuratov told a news conference.

In the most dramatic case, one of Russia's highest-ranking generals was dragged from hospital to prison last month to be interrogated on corruption charges including the allegation he accepted a luxurious country dacha from a military contractor.
General Konstantin Kobets, who defended Yeltsin during a hardline communist coup in August 1991, denied the charges and accused the president of using him as a scapegoat.

Reports of wide-scale corruption in the armed forces began to appear in the media in the early 1990s when huge quantities of arms and equipment went missing as the former Soviet army withdrew from eastern Europe.
But, in contrast to the Kremlin's current anti-corruption drive, aimed at all areas of government, no high-profile military figures from that period were ever formally charged.
